site.title: Technology Knowledge Base
site.what: A hands-on course in eight technologies for software engineers. Every lesson pairs a short explanation with code you run, change and test on your own Mac mini or Windows PC. Simulators replace hardware, and examples use open-source tools.
why: Learn by building: most of each lesson is a lab with real, tested output, not theory.
Grow in clear steps: L100 run it, L200 build it, L300 harden it, L400 design it, then a capstone that ties a topic together.
Stay honest: every lesson says what was actually run and what still needs a CI run on macOS or Windows.
Use AI safely: where a local model helps, it only proposes or explains; deterministic code makes the decision (the rule from the LPC1768 guide).
levels: Set up the tools and run a first example.
Copy, run and observe. Short explanations, small labs.
Change and combine working code; add one feature yourself (build task).
Break it on purpose with a realistic fault, then make it robust (failure lab).
Compare options with measurements, record the decision (ADR), guard it with a fitness test.
One end-to-end project per topic that reuses the earlier labs and prints a scorecard.
Undergraduate theory: theorems with proofs checked in code, problem sets, an ethics case study and a reading seminar.
Cross-topic projects: combine 2–3 topics into one system, test every seam between them, reproduce an integration failure and fix it.
site.howToUse: Pick a topic, read its 'What it is' and 'Why learn it', then follow the lessons in order. In each lesson: read the Concept, do the Lab, predict and check the Try it tasks, complete the Build task, and pass the Checkpoint. Use the Mac mini / Windows switch for commands.

quantum-computing.what: Quantum computing uses qubits and quantum gates to build circuits whose results are probabilities you sample. Today's machines are small and noisy, so practical work means writing, simulating, testing and benchmarking circuits on a classical computer.
why: Know what quantum computers can and cannot do today, and test claims with your own simulations instead of hype.
Learn the workflow used in practice: circuits in Qiskit or Cirq, portable OpenQASM, noise models and error mitigation.
Understand why post-quantum cryptography matters for software you maintain now.
usedFor: Planning the move to post-quantum cryptography
quantum-computing.capstone: A quantum optimisation service with a classical baseline, noise model, mitigation and an honest benchmark report.

cryptography.what: Applied cryptography is a set of vetted building blocks — hashes, MACs, encryption, signatures, key exchange, password hashing — that you combine to protect data. You do not invent them; you choose the right one and use it correctly.
why: Most security failures come from misusing good libraries (reused nonces, weak password storage, unchecked tokens), not from broken algorithms.
You will be able to protect data at rest and in transit, manage keys and certificates, and sign what you ship.
Prepare code for change: crypto agility and the move to post-quantum algorithms.
usedFor: TLS for web and API traffic
Signed software releases and package checks
cryptography.capstone: An encrypted document service with key rotation, a signed audit log, mTLS between components and a post-quantum hybrid option.

ai-agents.what: An AI agent is a program that lets a language model choose which of your functions (tools) to call, runs them, and feeds the results back until the task is done. The model proposes; your code executes, validates and enforces the rules.
why: Agents are being built everywhere; knowing the loop without a framework lets you judge any framework.
Run models locally on your Mac mini or Windows PC, keep data private and control cost.
Make agents safe and reliable: evaluations, tracing, budgets, approvals and defences against prompt injection.
usedFor: Assistants that call internal APIs and tools
ai-agents.capstone: An incident-triage agent with MCP tools, retrieval over runbooks, tracing, evaluations in CI and approval gates; policy code decides severity and actions.

distributed-systems.what: A distributed system is several programs (nodes) that cooperate only by sending messages over a network. Messages can be slow, lost or duplicated and every node has its own clock, so the system must keep working anyway.
why: Almost every modern application is distributed: services calling services, queues, replicated databases.
Learn the tactics that make calls safe — timeouts, retries with backoff, idempotency — and why each exists.
Reason about consistency, failures and scale with tests and simulations instead of guesses.
distributed-systems.capstone: An order pipeline with saga, outbox, idempotent consumers, tracing and backpressure, tested by a seeded chaos campaign.

application-architecture.what: Application architecture is the set of decisions about how an application is split into parts, how those parts depend on each other, and how it meets the outside world. The goal is practical: keep the code easy and safe to change as it grows.
why: Most long-term cost in software is change; good structure keeps change cheap.
Learn patterns you can apply in any language: layers, ports and adapters, modules, events, contracts.
Make decisions visible and checkable: diagrams as code, ADRs and fitness functions in CI.
application-architecture.capstone: Evolving one example (Library Loans) into a production-ready system: strangled module, tenancy, policy, events, SLOs, contract tests and fitness functions.

microbit.what: The BBC micro:bit is a small single-board computer with sensors, an LED grid, buttons and a radio. Here you program it in MicroPython using the official browser simulator, so no board is needed.
why: Learn embedded thinking — sense, decide, act in a loop — with instant feedback in the simulator.
Practise real device problems: unreliable radio, non-blocking firmware, power budgets, gateways to a PC.
Build an edge-to-cloud system where alarms stay deterministic and a local AI only explains (the LPC1768 guide's rule).
usedFor: Prototyping IoT ideas before using real hardware
microbit.capstone: A classroom environmental monitor network: several simulated boards, reliable radio, gateway, MQTT, dashboard, digital-twin drift check and local-agent explanations.

simulation.what: Simulation answers engineering questions by running a model of a system instead of the system itself — for example how many staff keep waiting times low, or how likely a project is to slip. Every model is state, a rule for change, a clock, and an experiment around it.
why: Test decisions safely and cheaply before changing a real system.
Turn uncertainty into numbers you can defend: confidence intervals, sensitivity, validation.
The same skills power capacity planning, risk estimates, digital twins and optimisation.
usedFor: Capacity planning for queues and services
Agent-based models of people or traffic
Digital twins fed by live data
simulation.capstone: A digital twin of a service centre: input modelling, discrete-event core, calibration, sensitivity, staffing optimised under an SLA, and a governance pack.

astronomy.what: Astronomy and astrophysics study objects beyond Earth — stars, planets, galaxies — and the physics that explains them. Here it is applied computing: you calculate where objects are in the sky, simulate orbits, and analyse images, catalogues and light curves the way observatories and surveys do, using simulators and open or synthetic data instead of a telescope.
why: Astronomy is a data science at scale: sky surveys produce huge images, catalogues and alert streams, and the same pipeline skills apply far beyond astronomy.
Learn exact, testable computing: coordinates, time scales, units and orbits have published reference values to check your code against.
Practise honest analysis: calibration, uncertainty, model comparison and reproducible pipelines, ending with a real exoplanet-search workflow.
usedFor: Planning observations and tracking objects in the sky
Processing telescope images and building catalogues
Finding exoplanets and variable stars in light curves
Real-time alerts for new events in large surveys
Testing physical models, such as dark matter in galaxy rotation curves
astronomy.capstone: An exoplanet transit search pipeline: light curves → detrend → period search → vetting → fit with uncertainty → report; a local agent explains candidates, code decides.

integrated.what: Eight projects that each combine two or three of the topics into one working system. Real systems fail at the boundaries between technologies, so every project names its seams, tests each one, and reproduces a failure that only appears because the topics meet.
why: Practise what real work looks like: cryptography inside a distributed system, an AI agent driving a simulator, a sensor fleet syncing to a backend.
Learn to find and test integration contracts, the place most production incidents start.
Reuse your earlier labs as components instead of starting from scratch.
usedFor: Reliable job platforms for scarce or noisy hardware
Safe tool use by AI agents
integrated.capstone: Each L600 project is its own capstone: a runnable system with a scorecard, seam tests, a reproducible failure lab, fitness functions and decision records.
